analysis.one_liner: Cuts off all federal money for carrying out the health care law and its companion education act.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any committee; it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred any federal money from being spent to carry out the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (the 2010 health care law) and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, which covered health financing changes and federal student lending. Cutting off funding would have stopped the law's coverage expansions, subsidies, and insurance rules from being put in place, without formally repealing the law itself. The bill was referred to six House committees and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the people who would have gained are those who bore the health care law's costs: high-income households subject to its Medicare surtaxes, and industries facing its taxes and requirements, such as medical device makers. At the same time, people who had not yet gotten coverage, subsidies, or protections under the law — uninsured people, people with pre-existing conditions, young adults on family plans — would have lost the benefits the law was phasing in, because the money to run them would have been cut off.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Opponents of the health care law

how_it_helps.text: Deauthorizing all funding would have prevented money from being spent to carry out the health care law — including the subsidies that help people buy insurance, the Medicaid expansion, and the new insurance rules — effectively freezing the law without formally repealing it.
It would have ended the flow of federal money for the education provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act, which included changes to federal student lending and aid.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen mainly on ordinary people: the uninsured and those awaiting the law's coverage expansions, subsidies, pre-existing condition protections, and dependent coverage would have had them frozen or never implemented. States, insurers, and employers that had begun implementing the law would have faced sudden uncertainty.

drawbacks.text: Cutting off all funding for the health care law would have halted coverage expansions, subsidies, and new protections, leaving people who had not yet gained coverage under the law without them.

Because much of the health care law's spending is mandatory rather than subject to annual appropriations, a deauthorization bill would not by itself have stopped the law from operating — the measure was largely a statement of opposition rather than a working repeal mechanism.
Suddenly freezing funding would have created uncertainty for states, insurers, employers, and individuals who had already begun complying with the law's requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's only benefit was to its supporters' goal of stopping the health care law, and even that was questionable: as a one-sentence deauthorization it would not have repealed the law or ended its mandatory spending, so its practical effect would have been limited and largely symbolic. The cost, if it had passed, would have fallen on people waiting for coverage, subsidies, and protections under the new law, and on the states, insurers, and businesses that had already begun implementing it. The bill's death in committee avoided that disruption at no cost to anyone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to six House committees and later to two subcommittees, none of which ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Graves of Georgia introduced the bill on July 27, 2010, with five other Georgia Republicans joining as original sponsors.
A total of 53 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The House referred the bill to six committees on the day it was introduced — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, and House Administration.

In October 2010 it was referred to two Education and Labor subcommittees, the last action of record; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
Because the bill only cut authorization for funding and did not repeal the laws themselves, much of the health care law's mandatory spending would have continued even had it passed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health care law kept operating and the coverage expansions it provided continued; the bill's sponsors and cosponsors lost nothing except a symbolic measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The health care law and its future enrollees

for.name: Rep. Tom Graves
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut off funding for the health care law and its companion act.

against.name: House Democratic majority (253 of 253 House Democrats)
against.role: Majority party controlling committee and floor agendas, 111th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda while the bill sat without a hearing in committee for the rest of the session.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Republican (53 of 178), and no Democrat signed on; the bill received no vote, so no roll-call record exists beyond party affiliation of its supporters.

industries.note: The bill would have blocked the health care law's revenue side, including the Medicare surtaxes on high earners and investment income and excise taxes such as those on medical devices and tanning services, sparing them the cost of the law.

Freezing the law would have halted the subsidized marketplaces and new customer mandates insurers were preparing for, while also stopping the insurer fee the law imposed. Ordinary people would have lost the coverage and subsidies that come with those marketplaces.

The 2010 reconciliation act shifted federal student lending to the Direct Loan program, ending subsidies to private lenders; cutting off funding for that act would have frozen the transition, though the lending statute itself would have remained on the books.
